content: Provider-assisted referrals are client-directed and occur within a timeframe that aligns with the client’s comfort level. Once partners are contacted, either by the client or by EDARP staff, they are referred to EDARP facilities for HIV testing services (HTS). Many EDARP clinics now offer early morning and late evening services to specifically target men and their partners. Contacts identified through partner services can access testing at these facilities. Challenges in delivering partner notification services (PNS) include clients’ reluctance to identify sexual partners involved in transactional relationships or those providing non-monetary support, as well as negative or hostile reactions from notified contacts. For clients who test negative, post-test services include tailored information about prevention services relevant to their needs. Among HIV-negative individuals identified through PNS, 21% are receiving PrEP. The World Health Organization (WHO) maintains a database of complaints related to in vitro diagnostics (IVDs) within the scope of WHO prequalification as part of post-market surveillance. IVD manufacturers are required to report serious and moderate complaints to WHO within specific timelines. Additionally, end-users can report complaints directly to WHO, which then informs the IVD manufacturer. WHO’s prequalification efforts focus on IVDs used in low-resource settings, supporting member states where preand post-market regulation for IVDs is underdeveloped. Since 2015, 113 complaints have been reported to WHO for HIV IVDs, with 32% classified as serious, 49% as moderate, and 19% as mild. An example of a complaint involved an NGO reporting that testing providers in a national program could not understand parts of the instructions for a new HIV rapid test due to text being in an unfamiliar language. The NGO assisted national authorities in reporting the issue to WHO, which informed the manufacturer. The root cause was identified as an editing error by a translation agency. The manufacturer issued corrected instructions and revised their standard operating procedures to include back-translation and proofreading by native speakers. A people-centered approach is essential for a successful HIV response. HIV diagnosis, care, and treatment services should be accessible, affordable, and tailored to the needs of vulnerable groups who may not typically seek care. This can be achieved through integrated service delivery at the primary healthcare level, addressing both health and psychosocial needs. Fragmentation of services for HIV, tuberculosis (TB), sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and mental health can be reduced through a one-stop shop model at the primary care level, facilitating diagnosis, treatment initiation, and ongoing care. The Odessa Test & Treat Clinic, using the AIDS Healthcare Foundation (AHF) model, provides integrated testing, treatment, and care services. The clinic offers same-day diagnosis and linkage to care, rapid testing, condom distribution, and counseling. Multiplex test kits are used to attract high-risk groups, and partner testing is available for individuals with HIV-positive partners. Lay provider testing and peer counseling have been piloted to increase demand for HIV testing, with services offered during evenings and weekends. The clinic also emphasizes rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) within 14 days of diagnosis and provides comprehensive services, including TB screening, reproductive health counseling, and cervical cancer screening. In Thailand, the Napneung program aimed to improve access to HIV testing and increase regular testing among at-risk individuals. Free, anonymous testing was provided in Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai by trained nurses and medical technologists. Outreach included distributing vouchers, posters, and online advertisements. Clients received preand post-test counseling and rapid testing for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C within one-hour sessions. HIV-positive individuals were immediately referred to partner hospitals for evaluation and treatment. In Indonesia, a joint service delivery strategy was implemented in 2018 to increase HIV testing coverage among TB patients. This included mobile HIV testing, assisted navigation by community-based personnel, specimen transport, and finger-prick HIV screening at primary care centers. Following 12 months of technical assistance, HIV testing coverage for TB patients rose from 47% to 93% at participating facilities. In Myanmar, Medical Action Myanmar (MAM) launched a harm reduction project in 2017 in remote areas like Putao, integrating HIV-related activities with existing malaria community health workers (CHWs). CHWs were trained to provide health education, needle exchange, and referrals for HIV testing and treatment. Mobile clinic teams supported CHWs, offering HIV testing, counseling, and linkage to care. This model effectively reached over 1,200 people who inject drugs, with 900 screened and treated for HIV, hepatitis, STIs, and TB. In India, PATH collaborated with local AIDS control societies to integrate HIV testing into private-sector TB care. Strategies included training private providers, establishing formal agreements for data reporting, and using link counselors to facilitate referrals for confirmatory testing and ART initiation. This approach increased HIV testing among private-sector TB patients, with 73% of notified TB patients tested for HIV. In Kenya, an integrated hypertension and HIV screening platform targeted men in informal workplaces and social venues. Mobile services were advertised through community channels and conducted during the day and at night. Offering non-stigmatizing hypertension services modestly increased HIV testing uptake among men. In Vietnam, Lighthouse introduced community-based HIV testing in 2016, using trained lay testers to provide accessible, stigma-free services. The initiative increased testing coverage and linkage to care, addressing barriers such as inconvenient clinic hours and discrimination in healthcare settings. This transformation maintains the detailed information while presenting it in a clear, professional manner.
